passages.happening:
‘Son of man,’ God says, ‘stand up on your feet and I will speak to you’ (verse 1). The Spirit enters Ezekiel and sets him on his feet (verse 2). God sends him ‘to the Israelites, to a rebellious nation that has rebelled against Me’ (verse 3), obstinate and stubborn. He is to say, ‘This is what the Lord GOD says’ (verse 4). Whether they listen or refuse, ‘they will know that a prophet has been among them’ (verse 5).

Three times God tells him not to be afraid, though ‘briers and thorns surround you, and you dwell among scorpions’ (verse 6). He must speak God's words whether they listen or not (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Son of man is God's ordinary name for Ezekiel, more than ninety times in the book. It means a mortal, a human being, standing before the glory of chapter 1.

The setting is still the summer of 593 BC. The exiles were hearing prophets who promised a quick end to Babylon's rule. Jeremiah, writing from Jerusalem at about this time, warned them not to believe those prophets. Ezekiel was sent to say the same unwelcome thing.

Prophesying could be dangerous. Jeremiah was beaten and imprisoned, and the prophet Uriah was killed by King Jehoiakim. Briers, thorns and scorpions picture a place that would wound Ezekiel at every step.
passages.later: God told Jeremiah the same thing at his call: ‘Do not be afraid of them, for I am with you to deliver you’ (Jeremiah 1:8). The prophet Uriah was put to death for his words (Jeremiah 26:20-23).
passages.hard:
Why would God send a prophet to people he knows will not listen?

The chapter does not promise that the hearers will repent. It says that, whether they listen or not, they will know a prophet has been among them. Several answers have been given. The message is a witness: when judgment comes, it cannot be mistaken for chance or for the defeat of Israel's God. A call to faithfulness rather than results protects the messenger from both despair and pride. The words describe the nation as a whole, and individuals could still respond; chapter 18 insists that anyone who turns will live. And the book looks past this generation to a day when God gives a new heart that will listen (36:26). The refusal of the hearers is not the end of the story.
passages.asks: Ezekiel was called to be faithful, not successful. Ask where you measure yourself only by results. And ask whom you need to keep speaking to, gently and truthfully, even if they do not listen.

passages.happening: ‘And you, son of man, listen to what I tell you. Do not be rebellious like that rebellious house. Open your mouth and eat what I give you’ (verse 8). Ezekiel sees a hand holding out a scroll (verse 9). It is unrolled before him, and ‘written on the front and back of it were words of lamentation, mourning, and woe’ (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Scrolls were sheets of papyrus or leather joined into long strips and rolled, and normally they were written only on the inside. A scroll written on both sides was unusual. It suggests a message so full there was no room left, and nothing Ezekiel could add of his own.

Lamentation, mourning and woe are funeral songs and cries of grief, the words of a coming disaster. Before Ezekiel can speak God's word, he must take it into himself. The prophet must not be like his hearers; the first test of obedience is his own.
passages.later: Jeremiah prayed, ‘Your words were found, and I ate them’ (Jeremiah 15:16). John was given a small scroll to eat, sweet in the mouth and bitter in the stomach (Revelation 10:9-10).
passages.asks: Ezekiel had to take in God's word before he could pass it on. Ask how you take Scripture into yourself, not just read it. And ask what hard word you may be avoiding.
